metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic, strictly on trials where TTB and Tallying make opposing predictions. Under the advocated TTB theory, subjects will generally choose the TTB-favored option, resulting in a metric close to 1. Under the competing Tallying theory, subjects will choose the Tallying-favored option, resulting in a metric close to 0. This maximizes the distance between the two theories.

The experimental design is structured such that in every trial, the option favored by Tallying (which wins on a greater number of lower-validity cues) is exactly the opposite of the option favored by Take The Best (which wins on the single highest-validity discriminating cue). By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic's prediction, we create a metric that will be near 1.0 for simulated Tallying agents and near 0.0 for simulated Take The Best agents, maximizing the discriminatory power between the two theories.

In all 6 trial types, the single highly valid feature (feature 1) favors one option, while the other 4 weakly valid features favor the competing option. WADD, even with heavy Laplace smoothing, assigns enough weight to the first feature (0.98 validity) to dominate the sum of the other four features, predicting that the subject will consistently choose the option favored by the first feature. Tallying, however, ignores validities and simply counts the number of positive features, predicting that the subject will consistently choose the option favored by the four weak features. Thus, measuring the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with a 1 on the first feature perfectly discriminates the two models (expected > 0.5 for WADD, < 0.5 for Tallying).

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chose the option favored by the single highly predictive feature (feature 1). By design, Tallying always prefers the option with more features, which in this experiment is always the option without feature 1. Therefore, Tallying will yield a metric value close to 0. WADD, on the other hand, weights features by their log-odds validity, causing the single highly predictive feature to dominate the weaker ones, resulting in a metric value close to 1.

Overload theory predicts pure random guessing on all trials, meaning the choice proportion for any trial type should be exactly 0.5 in expectation. Given 12 repetitions per trial type, the mean absolute deviation from 0.5 under Overload will be strictly governed by binomial noise (expected value ~0.113). In contrast, WADD predicts systematic deviations from 0.5 due to compensatory weighting of the smoothed validities, leading to choice proportions closer to 0 or 1. By computing the mean absolute deviation of choice proportions from 0.5 across unique trial types, we can cleanly separate the random guessing of Overload from the deterministic preferences of WADD.

Overload/Indifference Theory predicts random guessing (0.5) across all trials, completely ignoring cue values. WADD, on the other hand, evaluates the compensatory score of each option. On pure dominance trials (where one option has positive cues and the other has none, such as trials 1-4), WADD will strongly prefer the dominant option, while Overload/Indifference Theory will still predict a 50% choice rate. This metric calculates the proportion of dominant choices on these clear trials, ensuring a large and highly significant divergence between the two models.
